pending_items.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
pending_items.content:
Yemen's Houthi movement claimed responsibility for an attack on Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, on Wednesday, describing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi strikes that have killed scores of civilians.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the refinery attack caused fires and came in retaliation for the "brutal Saudi aggression against our country, including its targeting of passenger buses and citizens' trucks in the Al-Maqatirah district of Lahij, as well as other crimes in the capital, Sanaa, and the governorates."

The attack in the district of Lahij earlier this week killed at least 26 people.

In a follow-up post on X, Saree responded to Saudi threats to retaliate against Yemen's civilian Hodeidah port, which Saudi Arabia has already bombed, by warning that all "enemy Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will be targets".

"We warn employees, workers and those near these ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away, and we call on all shipping companies to remove their ships from those ports immediately," the post added.

Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, which controls the capital Sanaa and much of north and western Yemen, has been firing missiles at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July in a spillover from the Israeli-US war on Iran .

Riyadh broke the ceasefire, which also included Saudi Arabia, when it bombed Sanaa's international airport on 13 July.

Since then, the Saudi military has struggled to contain the Houthis and their ability to counter Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.

The ongoing attacks are wreaking havoc on the Saudi economy, oil infrastructure and the country's international image.

Airlines have cancelled international flights from the Saudi capital, Riyadh, while previous attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure have disrupted oil supplies.

The attacks have also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football's AFC Asian Cup and the flagship Future Investment Initiative conference.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudis said that air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in the country's Eastern Province. They did not deny that the attack had struck the oil refinery there.

Satellite images reviewed by Reuters showed large swathes of thick black smoke around the refinery, covering an area spanning around 600 square kilometres.

The Houthis have previously targeted Ras Tanura, which has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, during the conflict.

The refinery forms part of a strategic complex on the kingdom's Gulf coast facing Iran, through which the country exported most of its oil before the Israel-US war on Iran started on 28 February.

Since then, Saudi Arabia has had to send some of its oil through Yanbu on the west coast along the Red Sea, which receives oil via the East-West pipeline and has also faced attacks.

Separately, Houthi spokesman Saree had also said the group had attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases.

Saudi civil defence said a strike on Tuesday wounded 11 people at a tower in Riyadh’s financial district. The tallest building in the capital, the tower houses the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund, the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the tower in less than a week.

The first, on 19 November, damaged the building but caused no injuries. Saudi civil defence posted an image on Tuesday of the landmark tower showing some damage about halfway up the facade, similar to the impact of last week's attack.

pending_items.title: Netanyahu says corruption trial must end after court casts doubt on charges
pending_items.content:
Israel's caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday called for an immediate end to his long-running corruption trial after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping a case in which he is accused of bribery.

The judges' recommendations came as Israel's longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival after inconclusive October 27 elections.

Netanyahu's main rival Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a government and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.

"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family," Netanyahu said in a televised statement at parliament.

"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul. Who will give those years back to us?"

"The trial must end immediately," he added, saying the "fabricated cases" against him were falling apart.

During a hearing in Jerusalem on Wednesday regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.

In Case 4000, in which Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction.

That case is considered to be the most serious Netanyahu faces and concerns him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.

Netanyahu is alleged to have negotiated with Shaul Elovitch, the controlling shareholder of Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq, to get positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefiting Bezeq.

On Wednesday, Israeli media reported Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman as saying that proving the bribery charge in that case faced "considerable difficulties".

Netanyahu, who has been in power on and off for three decades, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and denounced the cases as a politically motivated plot against him.

He is the first sitting Israeli premier to stand trial.

Israel's Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who was unusually summoned to the hearing on Wednesday, said she would consider the judges' recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal.

In the second case, known as Case 2000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over allegedly negotiating with the owner of the Yediot Aharonot newspaper for favourable media coverage.

In exchange, Netanyahu allegedly raised the possibility of pushing for legislation to limit the circulation of Israel Hayom, a free newspaper that is the main rival to Yediot.

Judges on Wednesday questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct and recommended reconsidering the arguments in the case.

In a third case, Case 1000, Netanyahu faces fraud and breach of trust charges over allegedly receiving luxury gifts including cigars, champagne and jewellery from wealthy individuals in exchange for financial or personal favours.

Judges on Wednesday recommended finding an agreement in that case so it can be brought to a conclusion.

Netanyahu's right-wing allies immediately cheered the court's recommendations and demanded the trial be brought to an end.

"After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset," Israel Katz, who is the defence minister in Netanyahu's caretaker government, wrote on X.

Netanyahu's corruption trial opened in May 2020.

During his most recent term, which started in late 2022, Netanyahu proposed far-reaching judicial reforms that critics say sought to weaken the courts.

With coalition negotiations underway, Eisenkot's camp is already trying to start unravelling some of the Netanyahu-era judicial reforms in parliament.

US President Donald Trump had pushed Israeli President Isaac Herzog to issue Netanyahu a pardon.
